faq.a: Yes, cough is often absent; fever and systemic signs predominate.
faq.q: Can miliary TB present without cough?

faq.a: Yes, because HIV dramatically increases risk of dissemination.
faq.q: Is HIV testing mandatory in all cases?

faq.a: Use isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol for 6 months, but resistance risk is higher.

exam: A 5‑year‑old presents with fever, weight loss, and hepatosplenomegaly. Chest X‑ray shows diffuse micronodules. What is the most appropriate next step? — Obtain a Mantoux/IGRA and start empiric anti‑TB therapy while awaiting results.
A child with suspected miliary TB has a normal chest X‑ray. Which investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis? — PCR for MTB on blood or CSF.
You are treating a child with miliary TB who develops jaundice. Which drug should be stopped first? — Pyrazinamide, due to hepatotoxicity.
A patient with miliary TB shows sudden neurological decline. What is the most likely complication? — TB meningitis.
In a resource‑poor setting, sputum smear is negative but clinical suspicion is high. What is the recommended treatment strategy? — Start empirical 4‑drug regimen while arranging for culture/PCR.
A child on anti‑TB therapy develops visual blurring. Which drug is implicated? — Ethambutol; discontinue and monitor visual acuity.
ai.title: Miliary Tuberculosis in Children
ai.subject: Paediatrics
ai.summary: A disseminated form of TB where tiny foci spread via bloodstream. Presents with fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, and may involve meninges. Diagnosis relies on imaging, sputum, and clinical context.

b: Occurs in 5–10% of untreated TB cases in children
Can precede or coexist with TB meningitis
sections.p: Miliary TB is a hematogenous spread of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, producing innumerable micronodules in lungs and other organs. In children it often lacks classic pulmonary infiltrates.

t.b: Shows diffuse millet‑seed nodules; absence of consolidation suggests miliary pattern
Positive indicates TB exposure; negative does not exclude miliary disease in high‑risk settings
Often negative; a positive result confirms TB but is uncommon in children

t.a: PCR for MTB on blood or CSF
t.b: Detects DNA; a positive result supports diagnosis when imaging is equivocal

b: Stage I: Mild systemic symptoms, no organ failure
Stage II: Moderate symptoms, organ involvement (e.g., hepatosplenomegaly)
Stage III: Severe disease, respiratory distress, shock, or CNS involvement
sections.p: Severity is gauged by organ involvement and clinical stability. The WHO staging for TB in children classifies miliary disease as severe, requiring urgent treatment.

b: HIV infection – 30–50% of miliary TB cases in sub‑Saharan Africa
Malnutrition – impairs cell‑mediated immunity
Malaria – induces cytokine milieu favouring TB spread
sections.p: The primary cause is untreated or inadequately treated pulmonary TB. In low‑resource settings, HIV co‑infection, malnutrition, and malaria can precipitate dissemination.

t.b: Positive status increases risk of dissemination; a negative test does not rule it out

b: Fever >38°C, often intermittent
Weight loss or failure to thrive
Hepatosplenomegaly on palpation
CNS signs: neck stiffness, altered consciousness
sections.p: Children may appear ill‑appearing, with low‑grade fever, poor weight gain, and hepatosplenomegaly. CNS signs (headache, neck stiffness) hint at meningitis.

t.b: Detects meningeal irritation; a positive Kernig or Brudzinski sign raises suspicion of TB meningitis

b: Chest X‑ray – first line
Mantoux/IGRA – supportive
PCR on blood/CSF – confirmatory when available
sections.p: Investigation strategy balances availability and diagnostic yield. In resource‑poor settings, clinical judgment and basic imaging guide therapy.

t.b: Normal or minimal findings do not exclude miliary TB
High protein, low glucose, lymphocytic pleocytosis; confirms meningitis

b: Respiratory distress – consider ARDS
Shock – look for sepsis
CNS signs – suspect meningitis
sections.p: Rapid deterioration, respiratory failure, shock, or neurological decline necessitates immediate escalation.

t.b: Detects hypoxia and acidosis; indicates need for ventilation

b: First‑line drugs: isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol
sections.p: Treat the underlying TB with a standard 6‑month regimen, adjusting for drug availability and resistance patterns. Supportive care is crucial.

t.b: Inhibits mycolic acid synthesis; essential for sterilising activity
Broad‑spectrum bactericidal; avoid in patients with severe hepatic dysfunction
Potent against dormant bacilli; contraindicated in hepatic failure

b: Weekly review of weight and temperature
Monthly liver function tests if on pyrazinamide
sections.p: Monitor clinical response and drug toxicity. Prevent transmission with infection control and treat contacts.

b: Malaria – both cause fever and hepatosplenomegaly
Viral exanthem – rash may be present in TB but is less common
sections.p: Miliary TB can mimic viral exanthem, malaria, or fungal infections.

t.b: Negative in TB; positive indicates co‑infection

b: PCR may be negative if sample volume is low
sections.p: Low bacillary load may give false‑negative sputum smears; normal chest X‑ray does not exclude miliary disease.

t.b: Negative does not rule out TB in children
